scene.testo: Two days after the war in Europe ended, American air generals sat down across from Hermann Göring and asked him one question. When did you know the Luftwaffe was losing control of the air?
Göring did not name a battle. He did not name a defeat on any front. He named one German city. And that answer quietly contradicted an order he had given himself.
Across the table sat the general who had run the American air war over Germany in its final year. Carl Spaatz, commander of United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe.
Beside him sat Hoyt Vandenberg of the Ninth Air Force, Seventh Army commander Alexander Patch, and Alexander de Seversky, the aircraft designer who advised the Secretary of War.
The date was May 10, 1945. The questioning lasted two hours, and a military interpreter carried every answer into English. Göring had surrendered only days earlier, and been flown to Augsburg.

He had surrendered to the American 36th Infantry Division. He wore a gray uniform, stripped of decorations except the insignia of a Reichsmarschall. He had commanded the Luftwaffe since before the war began.
Now he had to explain to the men who beat him why they had won. He began by blaming someone else. In the early years, he said, he had definite plans.
Then, he said, in 1940, Hitler began to interfere. Spaatz let him talk. Then he asked the question he had come to ask. When did you realize you were losing control of the air?
Göring answered at once. When American long-range fighters could escort the bombers to Hanover, he said, and it was not long before they came to Berlin. One word. Hanover.

Not a battle. Not a front line. A city deep in northern Germany, far beyond the point where American escorts used to turn back. For Göring, that was the moment. Not when the bombers came. When the fighters came with them.

Through most of 1943, American bombers flew deep into Germany alone. Their escort fighters ran low on fuel and turned back near the border. From there to the target, the Flying Fortresses fought on their own.

German fighters waited for exactly that moment. In August, 376 Flying Fortresses struck the ball bearing plants at Schweinfurt. Albert Speer, the armaments minister, recorded a 38 percent drop in ball bearing production.
But the bombers paid for every mile they flew past the border. As long as they flew alone, the Luftwaffe could inflict losses on every raid. Then the escorts began to reach farther.

Joseph Goebbels, Hitler's propaganda minister, noticed it in his diary. At the end of September he wrote about a daytime raid on Emden. The Americans had flown with fighter escort, and suffered no heavy losses.

Five weeks later, the tone changed. In yesterday's daylight raid alone, he wrote, we lost thirty fighters. The Americans now came with fighter escort, carrying first-class equipment, and German fighters were no match.

It was deeply humiliating, he wrote, to watch the enemy lead us by the nose in the air war. That autumn, Göring's fighter general, Adolf Galland, reported American fighters shot down over Aachen, inside Germany.
Göring told him that was impossible, and issued a formal order that they had not been there. That scene is in our own video about Galland. Here it matters for one reason.

The man who had ordered the denial of those fighters in 1943 was now telling Americans that the same fighters decided the air war. Meanwhile, the Americans hung extra fuel tanks beneath their fighters.
Each month the escorts pushed deeper. Emden. Hanover. Then a new fighter, the P-51 Mustang, which could fly from England to Berlin and back with fuel left to fight.
By early March 1944, American fighters were flying over the capital of the Reich. It was not long before they came to Berlin, Göring told Spaatz. Then we knew we had to develop jet aircraft.
Jets were his hope. Spaatz asked whether the jet really had a chance of winning. Göring said he was still convinced of it. If only we had had four or five more months.

He spoke of underground factories and a plant that could build a thousand jets a month. Vandenberg asked the obvious question. With your oil shortage, could you have trained enough jet pilots? Göring said yes.
Underground oil plants, he said, would have supplied enough fuel. But his other answers that evening told a different story. Spaatz asked whether the bombing had hurt pilot training. Göring said yes.

The attacks on oil crippled training, he said, because new pilots were sent up without enough instruction, and were no match for your pilots. Spaatz's chief of staff, Edward Curtis, asked whether the Americans had chosen good targets.

Especially oil. Göring said yes, excellent. Whenever we began repairing an oil plant, you bombed it again before we had produced a single ton. The escorts protected the bombers. The bombers consumed the fuel.

Without fuel, new pilots never learned to fly well enough to fight the escorts. Vandenberg asked about New Year's Day 1945, when the Luftwaffe struck Allied airfields in one big morning attack. Why was it never repeated?

Göring gave a curt answer. Orders from the supreme command. Hitler said there was no point in bombing American planes, because more would come like bees. Hitler himself had called American production figures fairy tales.

Vandenberg then asked him to compare the air forces he had fought. Göring dismissed the Russians in a single sentence. On the Americans, he was precise. They were superior in technology and in production.

The pilots, he said, were equal. English, German and American airmen fought with the same skill. The difference was what stood behind them. Because our production capacity was not as great as America's, we could not build fast enough.

He added that the fighters overhead were demoralizing. After escorting the bombers, they dived down and hit everything, including jets as they landed. Spaatz sent the interrogation record to General Henry Arnold, with a short note.

I think you will find this most interesting, he wrote. After the war, Arnold published his memoirs and described the interrogation in detail. But de Seversky, who had sat at that table, noticed what was missing.

In 1950, he wrote that Arnold had omitted one passage. The question: when did you know you had lost control of the air? The answer: Hanover. A pity, de Seversky wrote, that Arnold left out this important paragraph.
A year and a half later, Göring was convicted at Nuremberg. He took his own life in his cell the night before his execution. In 1943, he had ordered that American fighters did not exist over Germany.
In May 1945, asked when he knew the air war was lost, he named the city those same fighters reached alongside the bombers. Subscribe, and tell us in the comments whose story we should tell next.

descrizione:
In May 1945, American air generals interrogated Hermann Göring and asked when he knew the Luftwaffe had lost control of the air. His answer was one German city: Hanover. This documentary follows the Göring interrogation by Carl Spaatz, the arrival of long-range American escort fighters, and what the Reichsmarschall admitted about oil, pilots and production.

We trace the daylight bombing campaign of 1943, the Schweinfurt raid, Goebbels's diary entries, the Aachen order given to Adolf Galland, and the rise of the P-51 Mustang over Berlin in 1944. Every detail comes from interrogation records, memoirs and documented history.

Watch to the end for the missing paragraph that de Seversky said General Arnold left out of his memoirs. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more firsthand accounts of the war.
